## Job Market Paper

### The Power of Sperner's Lemma in Fair Division

*Abstract*: This paper develops a general approach to fair and efficient division that does not rely on equilibrium existence. First, I show that when the set of feasible allocations is compact, convex, and invariant to permutations of agents, and utilities are continuous and concave, there exists an allocation that is envy-free and weak Pareto efficient. The result applies to both problems with divisible resources and to indivisible-resource problems after appropriate convexification. In particular, it applies to problems with infinite-dimensional allocation spaces. The proof searches over Pareto weights and uses a regularized weighted welfare problem together with Sperner's lemma to identify weights at which all agents are simultaneously envy-free.

Second, the same construction yields a computational counterpart: in finite-dimensional environments, stopping the Sperner procedure at finite resolution produces approximately envy-free and approximately weak Pareto-efficient allocations in polynomial time for a fixed number of agents, under suitable computational-access assumptions.

Third, I combine the infinite-dimensional existence result with the finite-dimensional algorithm to allocate fairly, efficiently, and dynamically. The problem of fairness and efficiency of dynamic allocations arises in transportation, infrastructure, natural-resource management, computing, and has been extensively studied in computer science and engineering. Yet these problems cannot be tackled by present-day economic fair-division techniques. I approximate infinite-horizon environments by increasingly rich finite-dimensional truncations and apply the algorithm to each truncation. The approximation error separates into an algorithmic component and a truncation component, which can be controlled independently. Because the computational cost grows polynomially with the finite-dimensional problem size for a fixed number of agents, this approximation scheme remains computationally meaningful as the horizon expands. Applications include transportation capacity, renewable-resource extraction rights, and computing capacity.

## Working Papers

### Fairness and Incentives in Combinatorial Assignment

*Abstract*: We consider the fair and efficient random assignment of indivisible goods subject to resource constraints. Agents receive bundles randomly, but individual lotteries over bundles that are feasible in expectation need not be jointly feasible. Consequently, we treat a lottery over feasible allocations as a public good. We show that every feasible finite economy admits an envy-free and Pareto efficient random assignment that may be supported as a Lindahl equilibrium. For a finite type space with specified expected utilities, we construct a mechanism whose outcomes are exactly feasible and Pareto efficient with respect to reported preferences. As the population grows and empirical type proportions and per-capita resources approach a limiting large economy, envy and gains from manipulation vanish. The approximate incentive compatibility of the mechanism holds for all type profiles that approximate the limiting economy. The argument combines sensitivity bounds for linear programs with proximity bounds between fractional and integer optima.

### Implementation in the Cake-Cutting Problem

*Abstract*: I establish an equivalence between lotteries over deterministic cake partitions and fractional cake allocations—partitions of unity. The former is a common tool for convexifying a set of deterministic allocations, while the latter is an insightful embedding used in mathematical fair division. By proving that these two objects are utility-equivalent, I provide an implementation foundation for a mathematical representation commonly used in fair division. In addition, I show that every simple partition of unity belongs to the convex hull of degenerate partitions of unity, which means it is implementable by a lottery with finite support.

## Work in progress

### Almost Marginal Product Allocations

*Abstract*: I investigate the limiting behavior of agents’ utilities along every sequence of Walrasian equilibrium under pointwise convergence of utilities to quasilinear utilities (small income effects). It turns out that the gap between equilibrium utilities and agents’ marginal contributions can remain strictly positive in the limit despite small income effects. Second, I provide a sufficient condition under which the gap goes to zero: equilibrium and welfare-maximizing allocations remain in a common compact interior region on which the utility gradients converge to quasilinear utility gradients.
